extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent prosecutors, patent attorneys, and judges evaluating §101/abstract-idea issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying when claimed subject matter is an abstract idea (judicial exception) under §101/Alice, with categories of abstract ideas, examples from case law, and explanatory notes on when computer implementation or conventional components do not impart eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to managing human behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to concepts that manage or guide human behavior (e.g., storing user-selected pre-set limits on spending and notifying the user when reached) are abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Intellectual Ventures I LLC v. Capital One Bank (tracking financial transactions/budgeting). The Federal Circuit described such claims as directed to ideas of organizing human activity; adding routine computer components (e.g., databases, notifications) does not make such claims patent-eligible. Other examples include content filtering (BASCOM) and mental processes used by neurologists (In re Meyer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to tracking or organizing information
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims involving collecting, classifying, storing, encoding/decoding, organizing information, or tailoring content based on user info/time are abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: BASCOM (filtering content), TLI Communications (classifying and storing digital images), Electric Power Group (collect/analyze/display results), RecogniCorp (encoding/decoding image data), Digitech (organizing information through mathematical correlations), Intellectual Ventures cases (receiving/screening/distributing email, tailoring web pages based on user info and navigation data). Presenting results of collection/analysis without identifying a particular tool for presentation remains abstract.

rubrics_metrics.name: An idea 'of itself' (an uninstantiated concept or mental process)
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea standing alone—an uninstantiated concept, plan, or scheme—or a mental process that can be performed in the human mind or with pen and paper, is an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase is used for ideas having no particular concrete or tangible form and for mental processes. Courts have held methods performable mentally (or equivalent to human mental work) are unpatentable abstract ideas. Collecting and analyzing information is treated as within the realm of abstract ideas because information is intangible; merely presenting results of such abstract processes is also abstract (cases: CyberSource, Electric Power Group, Content Extraction, Alice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to data comparisons performable mentally (mental processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that consist of obtaining, comparing, and using intangible data in ways that can be performed mentally (or with pencil and paper) are abstract mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CyberSource (verifying credit card transactions by mapping related transactions), University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry Genetics (comparing BRCA sequences and identifying differences), Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping/comparing loan packages). If nothing in the claim requires a computer or other non-mental implementation, the claim may be directed to a mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to organizing or analyzing information analogous to human mental work
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that organize, analyze, or translate information in ways that mirror human mental activity (even if aided by computers) are abstract when the claim could be performed mentally or with routine tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics (translating a functional description into hardware component description), Content Extraction (data collection, recognition, and storage analogous to human review and record-keeping), FairWarning (collecting and analyzing access logs to detect misuse). Courts have rejected arguments that computer processing of bit streams alone avoids abstraction when the claimed steps are those humans have long performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts described as ideas having no particular concrete or tangible form
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite combinations of steps amounting to an abstraction—an idea without a particular concrete or tangible form—are abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ultramercial (using advertising as exchange/currency), Versata (determining a price using organizational and product hierarchies described as a conceptual framework), In re Brown (assigning hair designs to balance head shape). Such building-block conceptual frameworks are treated as abstract ideas capable of mental performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding conventional computer components to well-known business practices is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely adding generic or conventional computer components to traditional business practices or human activities does not make a claim non-abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: claims described as 'adding conventional computer components to well-known business practices' (e.g., a device for a server taking orders) remain directed to an abstract idea when the underlying concept is an organization of human activity or business practice (see examples in multiple Federal Circuit decisions). Examiners and courts look for inventive concept beyond routine computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships/formulas as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical relationships, formulas, algorithms, and calculations are treated as abstract ideas (judicial exceptions) and may be non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts have characterized mathematical concepts—procedures for conversion, formulas for alarm limits, algorithms—as abstract ideas (Benson, Flook, Alice). Historically sometimes treated as laws of nature, more recent precedent characterizes them as abstract ideas. The presence of a mathematical formula in a claim may render it a judicial exception unless integrated into an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to a mathematical relationship or formula (specific formulas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims relying on a specific mathematical relationship or formula (e.g., Arrhenius equation for cure time) are judicial exceptions and can be non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Diamond v. Diehr noted that a mathematical formula is an exception (non-statutory) like a scientific principle or natural phenomenon. The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions have repeatedly treated specific formulas or algorithmic relationships as falling within the abstract-idea exception unless the claim contains inventive application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts relating to performing mathematical calculations (manipulating data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that amount to performing mathematical computations, manipulating numerical data, or organizing information through mathematical correlations are abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bancorp (calculations/manipulation in life insurance policy valuation), Digitech (manipulating existing information using mathematical formulas to create new organized data). Courts look to whether claimed computations are merely mathematical operations or whether they are applied in an inventive manner tied to a specific technological improvement.
